extracted.intended_audience: inventors, patent lawyers, and law students studying patentability principles
extracted.subtask_description: Rules and tests for what kinds of 'manufactures' (substances, machines, improvements, combinations, or methods embodied in tangible means) are patentable, and how prior use, specification, and claim scope affect validity. Focused on legal principles and case-based guidance for drafting and challenging patents.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior public use and disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject must not have been publicly used or made known before the patent; if it was used by others or by the patentee himself prior to the grant the patent will be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Text notes multiple cases: secret known only to a few but actually put into practice by one of them voided a later patent (Tennant/bleacher example). Public sale or exposure to sale before sealing (even by the inventor) makes the patent void (British imperial verdigris example). Mere private knowledge without publication may not constitute 'use' (Dr. Hall/object-glasses example), but actual making and public sale do. The chapter cites cases and warns that prior use by any person can invalidate a grant.

rubrics_metrics.name: First public communication determines inventor for simultaneous discoveries
rubrics_metrics.description: When several persons discover the same thing about the same time, the person who first makes the communication of it to the public is accounted the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by the statement that 'he is accounted the inventor who makes the first communication of it to the public' and the Dr. Hall example where mere private knowledge without publication did not defeat a later patentee. Practical implication: timing of disclosure/publication matters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental use prior to patent (uncertain safe harbor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Experiments made to try the efficacy or full extent of a discovery may or may not constitute a 'use' under the statute; the law has not decisively established how much experimental use is permitted without invalidating a subsequent patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text explicitly says it 'has not yet been decided' whether such experiments are a 'using' within the meaning of the statute and warns that it would be 'very difficult to say how much' can be used by way of experiment without risking invalidation. Practitioners should be cautious: substantial practical exploitation as 'experiment' risks being treated as public use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Must be vendible matter
rubrics_metrics.description: The subject of a patent must be vendible — something capable of being bartered in commerce — as opposed to mere knowledge or something to be learnt by practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rationale: patent statute is for encouragement of trade and commerce; if it cannot be sold, it is hard to justify monopolizing it. Judges' dicta support that 'manufacture' implies something vendible (Heath J., Kenyon C.J.). Use this test when assessing whether an alleged invention is properly a 'manufacture' rather than an abstract method or principle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material and useful (utility / public benefit)
rubrics_metrics.description: A new manufacture must be material and useful; it must be of some consequence in commerce and beneficial to the public — trivial or purely curious changes are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Courts will ask whether the invention is a 'material and useful' manufacture; cases (Manton v. Parker, Brunton v. Hawkes) show nonsuit where utility/purpose failed on experiment. The rule prevents monopolies for immaterial alterations (e.g., mere change of material or an unimportant novelty).

rubrics_metrics.name: Substitution of material or trivial form changes insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: The mere substitution of one material for another, or an immaterial change in form, is generally insufficient to support a patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: making an old machine of new materials (brass instead of wood) or changing form without substantial functional improvement will not be considered a patentable invention. The text warns against granting patents that would monopolize trivial curiosities and thereby impede future improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Machines and instruments as manufactures
rubrics_metrics.description: Any particular machine, engine, or instrument used in production of a substance is a 'manufacture' and may be patentable, provided its qualities satisfy the requirements of vendibility, utility, and substantial benefit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the machine produces an old article, it must make it cheaper or better; one of the machine's qualities should be pre‑eminent (very useful). The chapter cites authorities (Boulton v. Bull, Brown v. Moore) and emphasizes that mechanical inventions are proper subjects of patents when they yield new or improved practical results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Improvements or additions are patentable but must be claimed narrowly
rubrics_metrics.description: An addition to or improvement of a manufacture is recognized as a new manufacture in law and may be patented, but the patent must be confined to the addition or improvement itself and not extend to the whole underlying article.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Mansfield and subsequent cases permit patents for improvements, but if the grant extends to the whole (substratum) it is void (Jessop's case). The improvement must be substantial and useful; if it cannot be used without an existing grant, the patentee must wait to use it against that grant, although he may patent the improvement per se and sell it. Practically: draft claims/specification to focus on the improvement only.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations or arrangements of known things
rubrics_metrics.description: A new combination or arrangement of old materials or machines which produces a new effect (new article or a better/cheaper way of making an old article) may be patented; the novelty of the arrangement is the essential quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even when each part is old and separately in common use, the new compound or effect produced by combining them is what the grant protects. However, the patent must be for the new combination only; claiming the whole machine where only the combination is new will invalidate the patent (Browne/bobbin lace example). The specification must clearly express that the claim is limited to the new combination or application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must clearly confine claim to the new matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Where the patentable subject is an addition, improvement, or new combination, the specification must clearly express that the claim is in respect of that new combination or application only, and not claim merit in the original or old materials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lord Eldon and other authorities required explicit limiting language; failure to confine the claim to the addition/new combination can render the grant invalid. The text emphasizes that the ostensible object of the patent should be the new combined matter and not any part of the old article.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract principles or mere methods are not patentable unless embodied in tangible means
rubrics_metrics.description: A mere abstract or philosophical principle cannot be monopolized. A principle carried into practice by tangible means may be patentable, but the patent is, in reality, for the tangible means (substance or machine) enabling the method, not for the principle itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The better opinion cited is that a patent for the application of a principle is as bad as one for the principle itself; courts require a corporeal, substantial thing or a new mode of employing practical art. Cases (Boulton & Watt, Hornblower v. Boulton, King v. Wheeler) are cited. Practically: ensure patents claim concrete apparatus or composition, not a bare principle or broad method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patents must not claim more than inventor actually invented
rubrics_metrics.description: If a specification describes parts or combinations that existed before, and the patentee only invented a part or an improvement, claiming the whole invented machine or manufacture exceeds what was actually invented and may invalidate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Browne/Heathcote lace machine example shows courts will examine what the inventor actually invented versus what the specification claims. If the patentee 'took up his invention from a point' and then described a whole machine including old parts, his specification may be bad. Draft claims to match the inventor's real contribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combinations of proportions, quantities, times etc. may be patentable (subject to further rules)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations and proportions or timing in a process can be subjects of patents, though the text defers fuller treatment to a later chapter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chapter notes that point will be discussed elsewhere; current guidance is that such process limitations can be legal subjects but must meet the same requirements of novelty, utility, and adequate specification.
